title: Financial Statements of a Company
summary: Companies prepare their Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit and Loss in the format prescribed by Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013. This chapter is about knowing that format and placing every item under its correct major head and sub-head.

notes.heading: Meaning, objectives and components
notes.html:
Financial statements are the end products of the accounting process that report the financial position and performance of a company to its users. Under Section 2(40) they include:

  • Balance Sheet (position on a date)
  • Statement of Profit and Loss (performance for a period)
  • Cash Flow Statement
  • Statement of changes in equity (where applicable)
  • Notes to Accounts

Objectives: provide information about economic resources and obligations, earning capacity, cash flows, and help users take decisions and judge the effectiveness of management.

Limitations: historical cost based, ignore price-level changes and qualitative factors, affected by personal judgement (e.g. depreciation method), and can be window-dressed.

notes.heading: Current and non-current classification
notes.html:
• An item is current if it is expected to be realised or settled within 12 months from the Balance Sheet date or within the company's operating cycle, whichever is longer; or is held mainly for trading; or is cash or a cash equivalent.
  • Operating cycle = time between acquiring assets for processing and their realisation in cash. If it cannot be identified, it is assumed to be 12 months.
  • Everything else is non-current.

Example: operating cycle 15 months, a trade receivable due in 14 months is current; the same receivable with a 10-month cycle is non-current.

notes.heading: Statement of Profit and Loss (Schedule III, Part II)
notes.html:
ParticularsNote No.Amount
I. Revenue from Operations
II. Other Income
III. Total Income (I + II)
IV. Expenses:
Cost of Materials Consumed
Purchases of Stock-in-Trade
Changes in Inventories of Finished Goods, Work-in-Progress and Stock-in-Trade
Employee Benefits Expense
Finance Costs
Depreciation and Amortisation Expense
Other Expenses
Total Expenses
V. Profit before Tax (III − IV)
VI. Tax Expense
VII. Profit after Tax (V − VI)
  • Revenue from operations: sales of goods and services less returns; for a finance company, interest earned.
  • Other income: interest, dividend, profit on sale of assets, rent (for a non-finance company).
  • Cost of materials consumed = Opening raw material + Purchases − Closing raw material.
  • Changes in inventories = Opening − Closing inventory of finished goods, WIP and stock-in-trade.
  • Employee benefits: wages, salaries, bonus, PF contribution, staff welfare.
  • Finance costs: interest on loans and debentures, discount on issue written off. Bank charges go to Other Expenses.

notes.heading: Notes, contingent liabilities and common mistakes
notes.html:
• Notes to Accounts give the details of each line item and the accounting policies.
  • Contingent liabilities (claims not acknowledged as debt, guarantees given, bills discounted not yet matured) and commitments (uncalled liability on partly paid shares, capital contracts not executed) are not shown in the Balance Sheet; they are disclosed in the notes.
  • Share capital note shows Authorised, Issued, Subscribed (fully paid / not fully paid) capital with calls-in-arrears deducted and forfeited shares added.

Common mistakes: putting bank overdraft under trade payables; treating loose tools as fixed assets (they are inventories); putting bank charges under finance costs; showing provision for doubtful debts as a provision instead of deducting it from trade receivables; forgetting that current maturities of long-term debt are short-term borrowings.

keyTerms.definition: The schedule to the Companies Act, 2013 prescribing the form of a company's Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit and Loss.
Share capital plus reserves and surplus plus money received against share warrants.
Time between acquisition of assets for processing and their realisation in cash or cash equivalents.
Amounts payable for goods purchased or services received in the normal course of business: creditors and bills payable.
Amounts receivable for goods sold or services rendered in the normal course of business: debtors and bills receivable.
Short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of change in value.
Costs of borrowing, such as interest on loans and debentures.
A possible obligation depending on an uncertain future event; disclosed in notes, not in the Balance Sheet.

formulas.name: Cost of materials consumed
formulas.html: Opening inventory of materials + Purchases − Closing inventory of materials

formulas.name: Changes in inventories
formulas.html: Opening inventories − Closing inventories (finished goods, WIP, stock-in-trade)

mcqs.q: Securities Premium is shown in the Balance Sheet under
mcqs.explanation: It is a capital reserve shown under Shareholders' Funds → Reserves and Surplus.
Schedule III lists loose tools as a class of inventories.
It is a loan repayable on demand, hence a short-term borrowing.

mcqs.q: The operating cycle of a company is 16 months. Trade payables due in 14 months are classified as
mcqs.explanation: They are due within the operating cycle, which is longer than 12 months.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is shown under Finance Costs?
mcqs.explanation: Interest on borrowings is a finance cost; bank charges and audit fees are other expenses.

mcqs.q: Interest earned on loans by a company dealing in computers is
mcqs.explanation: For a non-finance company, interest is not from its main activity, so it is other income.

mcqs.q: A claim against the company not acknowledged as debt is
options: disclosed in the Notes to Accounts
mcqs.explanation: It is a contingent liability, disclosed only in the notes.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Calls-in-advance are shown under Other Current Liabilities.
Reason (R): Calls-in-advance are part of Subscribed Capital.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Calls-in-advance are a liability until the call is made; they are not part of share capital, so R is false.

questions.q: Under which major head and sub-head will 'Capital Work-in-Progress' be shown?
questions.answerHtml: Major head: Non-Current Assets. Sub-head: Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets → Capital Work-in-Progress.

questions.q: State any three limitations of financial statements.
questions.answerHtml:
• Historical cost: assets are shown at cost, not at current value, so price-level changes are ignored.
  • Qualitative factors ignored: quality of management, staff morale and reputation are not recorded.
  • Personal bias: choices such as depreciation method and inventory valuation affect the results.

questions.q: From the following, calculate Cost of Materials Consumed and Changes in Inventories: Opening raw material ₹40,000; Purchases of raw material ₹3,00,000; Closing raw material ₹60,000; Opening finished goods ₹50,000; Closing finished goods ₹35,000; Opening WIP ₹20,000; Closing WIP ₹25,000.
questions.answerHtml:
Cost of materials consumed = 40,000 + 3,00,000 − 60,000 = ₹2,80,000.

Changes in inventories:

  • Finished goods: 50,000 − 35,000 = 15,000
  • WIP: 20,000 − 25,000 = (5,000)

Total = ₹10,000 (added to expenses, since inventories have decreased).
